newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr spars with bears at $0.7830 barrier.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr spars with bears at $0.7830 barrier.

text.p: The Australian dollar kept a grip on 78 cents at the midsession but again faltered in the face of heavy offers, both actual and rumoured.

It started well enough after benign U.S. wages data made the market rein back its expectations for the likely extent of the U.S. tightening cycle. A widening A$ yield premium enticed a burst of Japanese demand which chased it as high as US$0.7830 resistance this morning, only to be engulfed by selling.
Nor was sentiment aided by a surprise A$103 million deficit on the balance of goods and services which pointed to a widening current account deficit and sluggish demand for imports.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local dollar had recoiled to US$0.7810/15 from the US$0.7830 peak and an early US$0.7816/21, but was still ahead of Tuesday's late US$0.7790/95.

Traders said there was much talk of hefty offers above US$0.7830 with rumour putting the sell orders in the billions. Some suspected the amounts were inflated by certain names who were very short of the dollar at levels much lower than here, but it had a cautionary effect all the same.
On the bid side, the demand from Tokyo for AUD/yen seemed genuine enough and there was an expectation of more to come this afternoon, so supporting the dollar.
The local currency was holding firm at 99.14/24 yen having pushed up from 98.67/77 late here Tuesday and was also 0.1 point higher on its trade weighted index at 60.7.

Dealers said Japanese investors had been big buyers of Australian government bonds in recent days and the trend looked set to continue after U.S. yields fell sharply overnight and the A$'s relative yield attraction improved as a result.

Many analysts felt the U.S. labour cost data alone would not be enough to prevent the Federal Reserve from hiking at its May 20 meeting, but it did suggest the absolute amount of tightening needed was less than previously thought.
That was bullish for the local dollar which had been in danger of seeing U.S. official rates surpass those here for the first time since the early 1980s.
However, there was yet a chance the Reserve Bank would decide to take further insurance out on the domestic recovery by easing Australian rates.

Today's trade data, while not directly relevant to monetary policy, did suggest domestic demand was muted in March and exports could be under pressure from the strong dollar. Goods exports slid nine percent, while total imports fell five percent and imports of consumption goods dropped seven percent.

Analysts emphasised it was difficult to draw conclusions from the volatile monthly trade data, but were interested to see if the softness in consumption imports was reflected in the retail sales data for March on Friday.
Elsewhere, recent speculation about the impending sale of three Federal airports was confirmed by Finance Minister John Fahey who said the government was close to a decision.

Rumour has valued the sale price as high as A$3.0 billion and, since the main bidding consortia include a large foreign presence, implies a possible net offshore need to buy A$ to pay for the airports. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
